summary: The build can start: Python, the DocumentDB MCP server and the documentdb-* agent skills are available, and Microsoft Learn docs confirm the platform APIs (mongoClusters, vector & full‑text search, AAD/OIDC support). Gaps that matter for the sample are: exact connection string/URI shape (SRV vs old host + port), which LLM / embedding model to pick (affects embedding dimension and vector-index params), a few local CLI tools (mongosh) are missing but have workable alternatives, and one Beanie-specific compatibility point (explicit Motor/Beanie version) could not be verified from installed skills/docs.
summary_points: Ready to start: python, node/npx, the documentdb MCP server and a full set of documentdb-* skills are installed and usable for build/verification.

Key cold-answer confusions found: resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), cluster is vCore/sku-billed (M30 etc.), DocumentDB supports built-in vector indexes (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) and a $search/$createSearchIndexes FTS engine — many cold answers described older Cosmos DB / other products.

Missing but non-blocking items: mongosh is not on PATH (use the documentdb MCP server or the Python driver for manual checks), and a local DocumentDB gateway isn't running (docker is available to run it).
Unverified/incomplete: exact Beanie + Motor / pinned driver versions for MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol (no authoritative doc found in the installed skills); the builder should pin/test versions.

Actionable guidance included for the builder to avoid using outdated Cosmos DB assumptions (connection URIs, billing, CLI groups) and to pick embedding model dimensions before creating vector indexes.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run sample code, create virtualenv, install packages (Beanie, Motor, LangChain, embeddings client), run seed & demo scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or verify the Python LangChain/Beanie sample.
tools.workaround: Install Python 3.10–3.13 and create a virtualenv. The machine inventory already has Python available.

tools.name: pip
tools.needed_for: Install Python dependencies (Beanie, motor, pymongo, langchain, embeddings client).
tools.detail: pip expected to be available in the virtualenv (run environment states pip works with the venv).
tools.workaround: Use ensurepip/venv to create a venv then pip; use system package manager to install pip if absent.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server (documentdb)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection: list databases/collections, sample documents, create indexes, run explain/aggregation and vector/full-text index commands to verify what the sample creates.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present in inventory with 18 data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, aggregate, explain_operation, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Would lose the authoritative machine-readable way to inspect the live cluster and verify created collections / indexes without using the Python driver directly.
tools.workaround: Use the Python driver (Motor/PyMongo) to inspect and manage collections/indexes, or run portal operations; but the MCP server is much more convenient for scripted verification.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn docs search & fetch)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative grounding for platform facts (resource types, vector & full-text search, connection strings, billing model).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to verify current recommendations and API shapes; builder would rely on local memory or third‑party docs.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal docs and product pages, or the DocumentDB MCP server for API-level tests; prefer to have learn available for canonical references.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, enable cluster preview features if necessary (FullTextSearch, change-streams for multishard), or read resource IDs when automating verification.
tools.detail: az installed; inventory shows azure CLI 2.89.1 with cosmosdb-preview extension present
tools.impact_if_missing: Unable to run control-plane commands from CLI; could still use portal or ARM/Bicep if available.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal or the azure MCP server tools to inspect/enable features.

tools.name: node / npx
tools.needed_for: If the builder adds or updates MCP skills or uses Node-based tooling; npx can install skill kits if required.
tools.detail: Node v24.21.0 and npx 11.19.0 are on PATH
tools.impact_if_missing: Less convenient for adding JS-based agent skills; not blocking for Python sample.
tools.workaround: Install Node/npm or run equivalent Python tooling; installed in inventory so no action needed.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optionally run a local DocumentDB gateway container for offline local development and integration testing (gateway image listens on port 10260).
tools.detail: Docker installed (version available in inventory) but run environment says no local DocumentDB gateway is running.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local DocumentDB gateway; must test against live cluster (which the run-environment allows).
tools.workaround: Use the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) per run environment or pull/run the local gateway container (see references).

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual interactive checks of the cluster (querying, index inspection) from a shell.
tools.impact_if_missing: Loss of a quick interactive verification path. Not blocking because the documentdb MCP server and Python driver can perform the same checks programmatically.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server tools and the Python Motor/PyMongo driver to inspect and exercise queries; install mongosh if preferred.

references.title: Quickstart examples showing MongoDB shell and SRV connection string

accelerators_missed: Local DocumentDB container (Gateway) — docker image available but gateway not running; start it with: docker run --rm -p 10260:10260 ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest (see documentdb-local-deployment guidance).

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) uses the provider namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB and the primary resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
confusions.grounded_answer: The modern Azure DocumentDB cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) uses the mongoClusters resource).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB documentation and resource types (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) describe Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resources; the new vCore Mongo clusters use a distinct resource type 'mongoClusters' under the same provider namespace, so the names overlap.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in IaC or CLI commands, they would call the wrong resource type and either fail or create a different Cosmos account; verification and any automated infra scaffolding would be incorrect.
improvements: Add a short prominent note on the top of the Cosmos DB / DocumentDB quickstart and ARM docs stating: 'For MongoDB vCore clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (az documentdb mongocluster / az cosmosdb mongocluster), not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.'
Update agent skill descriptions to explicitly show the new resource type and example CLI commands so agents don't fall back to old 'databaseAccounts' patterns.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group. Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create -n myAccount -g myResourceGroup --kind MongoDB. This is part of the core az CLI (az cosmosdb).
confusions.grounded_answer: The CLI exposes commands for mongoClusters under both az cosmosdb mongocluster and az documentdb mongocluster (documentdb command group includes mongocluster preview commands). Use the mongocluster subcommands (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create or az cosmosdb mongocluster create) as appropriate; these commands are in the CLI and may require the cosmosdb/documentdb extension for the preview features.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
az cosmosdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The 'az cosmosdb' group historically managed databaseAccounts and Cosmos DB APIs; newer mongoClusters commands exist under documentdb and cosmosdb groups and may be delivered via CLI extensions/previews, leading to ambiguity.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create with --kind MongoDB targets the older databaseAccounts flow (Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts'); the user could attempt to create the wrong resource model or miss mongoClusters-specific parameters (vCore, shard-node-tier, server-version).
improvements: Document and surface the preferred CLI group for mongoClusters in the sample README: recommend using az documentdb mongocluster create (or az cosmosdb mongocluster create) and, if necessary, instruct the builder to install/enable the cosmosdb/documentdb CLI extension.
Add examples showing both forms (az documentdb mongocluster and az cosmosdb mongocluster) and a note about preview/extension requirements.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.grounded_answer: Deploy mongoClusters with the Bicep / ARM resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (and corresponding Terraform/AzAPI module or Azure Verified Modules for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)
AVM module: Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB examples and many templates use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; the new managed MongoDB (vCore) offering uses a dedicated mongoClusters resource type under the same provider namespace.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses databaseAccounts in IaC, they'll deploy or expect a different resource model and miss mongoClusters-specific parameters; automated validation and example ARM/Bicep code would be wrong.
improvements: Add a Bicep snippet in the sample README showing Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters usage and reference the AVM module for vCore clusters.
Update any agent skill that currently points to databaseAccounts examples to include mongoClusters examples.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a MongoDB URI. Example: mongodb://username:password@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myaccount@. Port 10255 (TLS) and ssl=true (TLS/SSL) are required for Cosmos DB Mongo API endpoints.
confusions.grounded_answer: Mongo URIs for modern Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters typically use SRV form (mongodb+srv://<user>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000) or, for query-from-any-node, per-node ports starting at 10260; TLS (tls=true) and appropriate authMechanism (SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC for AAD) are required. The older documents.azure.com:10255 pattern applies to legacy Cosmos DB databaseAccounts, not to mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB (ports start at 10260)
Get mongo cluster connection strings (Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB Mongo API connection examples used the documents.azure.com host and port 10255. The new mongoClusters use different hostnames (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com), SRV records, and different port patterns (10260+ when query-from-any-node is enabled).

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo connection examples using documents.azure.com:10255

confusions.build_risk: If the builder hardcodes port 10255 and the documents.azure.com host, the client may fail to connect to a mongoClusters cluster (SRV-based), or it may choose wrong connection options and fail authentication or topology discovery.
improvements: Update quickstart README and sample .env.example to show the recommended SRV connection string format (mongodb+srv://...) and link to the 'Get the MongoDB connection string' doc.

Add a short note in the agent kit/documentdb-mcp-setup skill warning agents not to assume documents.azure.com:10255 for mongoClusters and to prefer the cluster's SRV connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is provisioned/billed in request units (RUs) per second (provisioned or autoscale provisioned throughput) or using the serverless option where available. It's RU-based rather than a vCore billing model for the Cosmos DB/Mongo-compatible offering.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (MongoDB vCore / 'Azure DocumentDB' offering) is billed by compute tier (vCores/sku like 'M30') and storage; it is not RU-based. Compute and storage are billed separately and you choose cluster tier (M-series) and storage size.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) cluster Bicep examples (sku M30)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB (Core API and some Mongo API offerings) and Cosmos DB for NoSQL used RU models; the vCore MongoDB offering (mongoClusters) uses vCore/compute tiers and storage billing.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB databaseAccounts RU-based billing pages (older Cosmos DB docs)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder sizes indexes or writes provisioning automation assuming RU-based quotas, they'd pick wrong capacity parameters (and the sample README would misinform users about cost/scale).
improvements: Add a clear billing note in the sample README: 'This sample uses a vCore-based cluster (M-series). Do not attempt to provision RU throughput-based accounts for the vCore offering.'
Add a short faq item in the agent kit distinguishing 'DocumentDB (vCore)' vs the older Cosmos DB RU model.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB-compatible endpoint you authenticate with MongoDB-style credentials (username/password). Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) authentication for the MongoDB API is not generally available; use account/database credentials (SCRAM).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM credentials and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) OIDC authentication for mongoClusters. The docs show an OIDC-style SRV URI example (mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC... ) for using managed identities and role-based access.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB docs often emphasized account-key/SCRAM authentication; more recent mongoClusters/DocumentDB features add Microsoft Entra ID/OIDC authentication and managed-identity support.

confusion_sources.title: Legacy guidance focusing on account keys and SCRAM

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD/OIDC is not available, they might not implement or document a secure AAD-based flow for in‑Azure apps (managed identity), missing recommended best practice for production deployments.
improvements: Add a short 'Authentication options' subsection in the sample README describing: SCRAM for username/password, and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for managed identity/VM scenarios, with example connection URIs and links to the AAD doc.
Update the documentdb-mcp-setup skill to include explicit steps for registering managed identities and constructing the MONGODB-OIDC connection string.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for sync, motor for async). For Python + Beanie ODM, use motor (Beanie runs on top of motor). There is a separate azure-cosmos SDK but that is for the SQL/Core API, not for MongoDB-compatible endpoints.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo / Motor). For async Python and Beanie ODM, Motor is the correct driver. The azure-cosmos SDK is for Cosmos DB Core/NoSQL; it isn't the right choice for the MongoDB wire-protocol endpoints.

grounding_links.title: Driver Best Practices — Azure DocumentDB (documentdb-driver skill)
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python (examples using MongoClient/mongodb+srv)

confusions.build_risk: None if the builder uses Motor for async Beanie flows; risk if using azure-cosmos for MongoDB endpoints (wrong API).

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API does not provide first-class vector index types (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) via MongoDB createIndex; vector indexes are not a built-in Mongo API feature.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides first-class vector index types (vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann). You create them with createIndexes and cosmosSearchOptions (or specific createIndex templates) and query them with the $search aggregation stage using the cosmosSearch operator. DiskANN/HNSW/IVF are supported with tunable parameters (dimensions, numLists, lBuild, maxDegree etc.).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search docs)
Quickstart: Use vector search with Node.js in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API had no integrated vector engine; the new DocumentDB offering integrates vector indexes into the Mongo-compatible surface, causing confusion with older pages.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no native vector indexes, they might implement a separate vector store and ETL, increasing complexity and cost unnecessarily.
improvements: Add a short example in the sample README showing how to create a DiskANN/HNSW/IVF index (JSON createIndexes template) and how to run a $search cosmosSearch vector query with a sample embedding.
Document the dependence between embedding model dimension and vector-index 'dimensions' parameter.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text / hybrid search is done by integrating the database with Azure Cognitive Search or by using MongoDB-native text indexes; for advanced full-text / semantic search you'd integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or a dedicated vector/search service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB exposes a built-in full-text search engine (BM25) created with createSearchIndexes and queried with $search, and hybrid search is supported server-side by combining BM25 search indexes and the integrated vector engine (cosmosSearch) with server-side Reciprocal Rank Fusion or $unionWith; no external Cognitive Search/ETL is required.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically users integrated Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search for advanced search; newer DocumentDB includes an integrated full-text engine and the ability to combine BM25 + vector directly, making the older integration guidance incomplete.

confusion_sources.title: Guidance that recommends Azure Cognitive Search for Cosmos DB full-text scenarios

confusions.build_risk: If the builder chooses to route text search to an external Cognitive Search service, they will add unnecessary complexity and cost, and miss the integrated hybrid retrieval patterns supported by DocumentDB.
improvements: Add an example in the sample README showing: createSearchIndexes for BM25, vector index creation, and a combined pipeline using server-side RRF (or $unionWith) so sample authors see how to implement hybrid search in-place.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports a subset of MongoDB server versions (historically 3.2 → 4.x etc.) and has feature gaps including server-side JavaScript/$where, some aggregation stages, and limited transactions/change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed MongoDB-compatible offering) supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions (5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0) and implements a high percentage of MongoDB operators (99.03% compatibility); some administrative or low-level operations are restricted (service manages plan cache, certain diagnostic commands, and some low-level aggregation operators) — check the compatibility matrix for exact operator support.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (wire protocol support)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflected older compatibility snapshots; the current service supports several modern wire protocol versions and documents supported/unsupported operators explicitly.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a limited older server version, they may avoid using modern Mongo features (or pick driver versions incompatible with the cluster), causing wasted development time or runtime failures.
improvements: In the sample README, recommend testing the target MongoDB driver version against the cluster and include a link to the 'compatibility-query-language' page so implementers verify specific operators they rely on.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Linux Docker image) which exposes the SQL gateway typically on port 8081. The emulator historically does not fully support the MongoDB API, so for MongoDB API development you usually test against a real cloud account or a local MongoDB server (mongo:latest) on port 27017.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) for local DocumentDB development; it exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (TLS). The documentdb-local-deployment skill documents using the Gateway image on port 10260 and the TLS/SCRAM setup for local dev.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
Local Gateway: Gateway image and port 10260 (learn docs referenced by skill)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB Emulator and generic guidance about using a plain mongo:latest container leads authors to assume the emulator is the right choice; DocumentDB provides its own local Gateway image tuned for the service and that gateway uses port 10260.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the Cosmos DB SQL emulator or a plain Mongo image without the DocumentDB Gateway, they will experience feature mismatches (vector / full-text search, SRV, TLS and auth differences) and tests may pass locally but fail on the live cluster or vice versa.
improvements: Add a 'Local development' section to the sample README explaining how to start the DocumentDB Gateway container and pointing to the documentdb-local-deployment skill for TLS and seed-data guidance.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB provides a Change Feed (Core API) for change notifications. The MongoDB-style change streams are not universally supported on the Cosmos Mongo API; if you need change events you typically use Cosmos DB Change Feed.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB-style change streams; the docs show change stream usage and explain that for some multi-shard scenarios you may need to enable a feature in the portal (preview toggle) for multishard/cluster-wide streams. The change streams API is the mechanism to read changes and is supported for migration and application patterns.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Change streams in Azure Cosmos DB's API for MongoDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older instructions emphasized Cosmos DB Change Feed (Core API) as the first-class streaming primitive. The MongoDB-wire compatible DocumentDB clusters offer Mongo-style change streams alongside change feed semantics; for cluster-wide features a preview flag may be needed.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unavailable, they might build a more complex polling/migration path or fail to implement recommended online migration or reactive features.
improvements: In the agent skills and sample README, add a short note: 'Change streams are supported — see the change streams doc and enable any required preview feature for multishard cluster-wide streams.'

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: I expect the service-specific MCP server is named documentdb (the MCP server that knows Cosmos DB / DocumentDB specifics). The general Azure MCP server provides generic ARM/resource actions, but data-plane inspection (collection/index introspection) is provided by the documentdb MCP agent/tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list databases, create indexes, aggregate, explain) for Azure DocumentDB. The general azure MCP server provides control-plane/ARM operations and best-practice lookups; both are available and complement each other.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (from inventory)
azure MCP server (control-plane)

confusions.build_risk: None; both MCP servers are present in the inventory and usable.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name for what is now Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB evolved into Cosmos DB). The managed service is Microsoft Azure's proprietary Cosmos DB engine; it is not the same as any similarly named open-source 'DocumentDB' projects. The Cosmos DB MongoDB API is a compatibility layer.
confusions.grounded_answer: Microsoft's naming is confusing: the 'Azure DocumentDB' name has been used historically, Cosmos DB is the later global brand, and the current 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' (the vCore offering) is a distinct managed MongoDB-compatible service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the project with that name). The managed service is Microsoft-provided; it is not Amazon DocumentDB. The docs explicitly explain the naming and relationship.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.build_risk: Minimal if documentation uses correct names; risk is user confusion if documentation mixes 'DocumentDB' with Amazon DocumentDB or older Cosmos DB names.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming' paragraph in the sample README clarifying the difference between 'Azure DocumentDB (this product)', 'Azure Cosmos DB (older brand)', and 'Amazon DocumentDB (AWS)'.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed engine (not a stock mongod). A MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility layer translates requests to Cosmos. Application code can usually use standard MongoDB drivers, but must account for behavioral differences and unsupported Mongo features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the managed MongoDB-compatible offering) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (the product's engine), and exposes a MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility layer. Application code generally uses standard MongoDB drivers without a service-specific SDK, but developers must be aware of documented compatibility details and operator differences.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming & engine info)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer treated the service as the earlier 'Cosmos DB' proprietary engine; current DocumentDB uses the open-source DocumentDB engine and a compatible layer, so the implementation detail differs.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Cosmos DB internals, they might choose inappropriate client behavior or miss engine-specific capabilities documented for DocumentDB.
improvements: Add a single-line clarification in the sample README: 'This service is backed by the open-source DocumentDB engine; standard Mongo drivers work, but please consult the compatibility matrix for differences.'

confusions.question: Which database name will this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_fintech_10 for all data created by the sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: The run environment explicitly requires the sample to use database sample_fintech_10.

grounding_links.title: Run environment (skill_md)

confusions.question: How will Beanie connect to the DocumentDB cluster from Python?
confusions.cold_answer: Beanie uses an async Motor (MotorClient) connection: AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']); await init_beanie(database=client.get_database('sample_fintech_10'), document_models=[ExpenseReport]).
confusions.grounded_answer: We could not verify a Microsoft Learn or installed-skill page that explicitly documents Beanie usage for Azure DocumentDB; using Motor as the async client for Beanie is the normal Beanie pattern, but no installed skill or Learn page in the environment explicitly states Beanie + Motor + Azure DocumentDB together.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The installed documentdb-driver skill documents driver best practices and the general pattern of using Motor for async Python, but none of the available skills or docs explicitly mention Beanie integration with Azure DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder picks driver versions that are incompatible with Beanie/Motor against MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol, runtime errors or subtle bugs may occur (connection options, TLS, authMechanism).
improvements: Add an example Beanie + Motor snippet in the agent kit or sample README (exact pins for motor/pymongo/beanie tested against MongoDB 7.0) so builders have a tested configuration to start from.

confusions.question: Where must the cluster connection string come from in the sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the cluster MongoDB connection URI at runtime from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI; never write credentials to files or check them into source control.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is confirmed by the run environment: the connection string is in DOCUMENTDB_URI and must be read from the environment at runtime and not checked into source control.

grounding_links.title: Run environment (skill_md)

confusions.question: What TLS/port constraints must the sample's Mongo client obey when connecting to the cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: The driver must connect over TLS/SSL and use the TLS port (typically 10255 for Cosmos DB Mongo endpoints). Include ssl=true (or tls=true) in the Mongo URI and ensure the client trusts the server certificate (provide CA or set tlsAllowInvalidCertificates only for local testing).
confusions.grounded_answer: TLS is required (tls=true). For modern mongoClusters the common connection pattern is SRV (mongodb+srv...) which embeds host and port; when query-from-any-node is enabled drivers may discover per-node ports starting at 10260. The older port 10255 on documents.azure.com is for legacy Cosmos 'databaseAccounts' endpoints and is not the canonical port for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB (ports start at 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer quoted ports used by older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts; the new mongoClusters use SRV hostnames and different port semantics (10260+ for node-per-port).
confusions.build_risk: Hardcoding port 10255 may cause connection failures to a mongoClusters cluster; the builder must prefer the provided SRV URI in DOCUMENTDB_URI or handle per-node ports dynamically.
improvements: In the sample README, show how to consume a mongodb+srv URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI and include a short note about query-from-any-node ports (10260+) for local or advanced topologies.

information_gaps.title: LLM and embeddings model choice & embedding dimension
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt did not specify which LLM provider and which embedding model to use (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Hugging Face, dimensions). This determines embedding vector size and therefore the 'dimensions' parameter when creating vector indexes. I searched Microsoft Learn and the installed skills (vector-search, documentdb-vector-search) for prescriptive model recommendations but found no concrete, service‑level default embedding model or exact dimension to pick for this sample. The builder must choose and document the model and embedding dimension before creating vector indexes.

information_gaps.title: Beanie + Motor + PyMongo version compatibility with MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol
information_gaps.description: No installed skill or Learn page in the inventory explicitly documents tested version pins for Beanie + Motor + PyMongo against Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters (MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol). The documentdb-driver skill gives best practices (singleton client) but does not supply exact version combinations to pin. The builder must pick and test driver/Beanie versions locally or add a note in the README.

information_gaps.title: Seed data content and size
information_gaps.description: The prompt leaves sample data shape and volume unspecified. The run environment requires a seed script but doesn't define how many reports, realistic fields, or idempotency contract. The installed skills advise on data modeling; none provide the precise sample dataset the sample should load. The builder must define sample report shapes and provide an idempotent seeder.

information_gaps.title: LangChain integration pattern for agent memory with Beanie
information_gaps.description: No installed skill documents a canonical pattern for coupling LangChain agent memory with Beanie ODM (persisting consistent categorisation decisions across a session). The vector-search and full-text skills discuss retrieval and vector storage, but not LangChain agent-memory storage specifics in combination with Beanie models. The builder must pick an agent memory implementation and document how it persists decisions (in-memory with optional DB persistence).

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) for cluster-related IaC, CLI and Bicep/ARM snippets; reference the mongoClusters docs when adding any deployment examples.

Consume the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and prefer the SRV form (mongodb+srv://...) — do not hardcode documents.azure.com:10255. Parse and pass tls=true and the recommended authMechanism (SCRAM-SHA-256 or MONGODB-OIDC for managed identity) to the Motor/Mongo client.
